title: Cache Really Matters
description: What a cache is, where it shows up, and how write-through, write-back, and write-around trade speed, consistency, and data-loss risk.
author: Pawan Bisht

blocks.text: A cache is a small, fast storage layer that keeps a copy of frequently or recently used data, so future requests for that data can be served faster than fetching it from the original (slower) source.

items: CPU cache (L1/L2/L3) — stores data close to the processor so it doesn't have to fetch from RAM every time.
Browser cache — stores web page assets (images, CSS, JS) locally so a page loads faster on repeat visits.
DNS cache — stores resolved domain-to-IP mappings so lookups aren't repeated.
Database/query cache — stores results of expensive queries.
CDN (Content Delivery Network) — caches content geographically closer to users.
Application-level cache (e.g., Redis, Memcached) — stores computed results or session data in memory.

blocks.text: Data is written to both the cache and the main database at the same time (synchronously), before the write is considered complete.

items: App writes data
Data is written to the cache
Data is immediately also written to the database.
Only after both succeed does the app get a write successful response.

left.title: Pros
points: Cache and database are always in sync - strong consistency
No data loss risk, since the database is updated immediately

right.title: Cons
points: Slower writes, since every write waits on the (slower) database too.
The cache gets filled with data that may never be read again, wasting cache space.

blocks.title: Good For:
blocks.text: systems where consistency matters more than write speed — e.g., banking or inventory systems.
Data is written only to the cache first, and the database is updated later, asynchronously — usually in a batch, or after a delay.

items: App writes data to the cache.
App immediately gets a success response — it doesn't wait for the database.
In the background, the cache periodically flushes changes to the database.
Multiple writes can be grouped together and written to the database in a batch.

left.title: Pros
points: Very fast writes, since the app doesn't wait on the slower database.
Reduces database load by batching multiple writes together.

right.title: Cons
points: Risk of data loss if the cache crashes before the async flush happens.
Cache and database can temporarily be out of sync.
More complex to implement because it needs a reliable flush or synchronization mechanism.

blocks.title: Good For:
blocks.text: high-throughput systems where speed matters more than instant durability — e.g., analytics counters, logging systems, metrics, or social media like counts.
Data is written directly to the database, bypassing the cache entirely. The cache is updated later when that data is read.

items: App writes data directly to the database.
The cache is not updated at write time.
When the data is requested later, the cache is checked first.
If the data is not in the cache, it results in a cache miss.
The data is fetched from the database and then stored in the cache.

left.title: Pros
points: Avoids filling the cache with data that might not be read soon.
Reduces cache pollution from write-heavy workloads.
Keeps the cache focused on data that is actually being read.

right.title: Cons
points: The first read after a write is usually a cache miss and is therefore slower.
Cache can briefly serve stale data if something else already cached the old value.
The cache is not populated at write time.

blocks.title: Good For:
blocks.text: write-heavy workloads where written data isn't immediately re-read — e.g., logging, bulk data ingestion, or systems where newly written data is rarely accessed immediately.
